hints: Start from argon core with 11 outer electrons to place, and recall why copper does not follow the simple 4s2 3d9 pattern.
Remember that when a transition metal forms a positive ion, electrons are removed from the 4s orbital before the 3d orbitals.
walkthrough:
Build the copper atom around stability**
Copper has atomic number 29, so after $[\text{Ar}]$ you have 11 electrons left. You might expect $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^94\text{s}^2$, but a full 3d subshell is extra stable. One 4s electron promotes to give $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^{10}4\text{s}^1$. Think of it as nature preferring a full d set plus a half filled s.

Form Cu2+ by removing 4s first**
When copper ionises, the 4s electrons are lost first because once occupied, the 4s level is higher in energy than 3d in the ion. Remove the single $4\text{s}^1$ electron and then one $3\text{d}$ electron to make the 2+ charge. That leaves $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^9$ with an empty 4s.

Final answer: copper atom: $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^{10}4\text{s}^1$
$\text{Cu}^{2+}$: $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^9$

hints: Focus on what changes around the central Cu2+ ion, water ligands are replaced by chloride ligands with no change in oxidation state.
walkthrough:
Spot what is swapped**
Look at the centre. $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ stays as $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, so this is not redox and not acid base. Six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are swapped out and four $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands swap in. Whenever one set of ligands directly replaces another at the same metal centre, we call it ligand exchange or substitution.
Final answer: ligand exchange / ligand substitution / ligand replacement

hints: Recall the familiar colour of aqueous copper(II) sulfate solution and the colour seen when concentrated HCl is added to it.
walkthrough:
Link each formula to its classic colour**
The hexaaqua copper(II) ion is the beautiful blue you see in copper sulfate solution. When excess chloride replaces water to give the tetrachlorocuprate(II) ion, the d-orbital splitting changes and the transmitted colour shifts to yellow, often seen as yellow-green in mixture. So blue turns to yellow-green.
Final answer: $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ blue and $[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$ yellow / green (yellow-green accepted)

hints: Count the ligands in $[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$ and recall the two possible shapes for coordination number 4, then pick the one favoured by large identical Cl- ligands.
walkthrough:
Use coordination number to fix shape**
$[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$ has four $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands, so coordination number is 4. For four bulky, identical, negatively charged ligands, repulsion is minimised in a tetrahedral arrangement around $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.

hints: Write products over reactants with powers equal to stoichiometric coefficients, remembering that water as solvent is omitted from Kstab.
walkthrough:
Assemble the Kstab expression**
Stability constants work just like Kc but water is left out because its concentration is effectively constant. Put the substituted complex on top: $$K_{\text{stab}} = \frac{[\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^4}$$ Note the power 4 on $[\text{Cl}^-]$ from $4\text{Cl}^-$ in the equation, and no $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ term.
Final answer: $K_{\text{stab}} = \dfrac{[\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^4}$

hints: Break the word bidentate into bi meaning two and dentate meaning teeth or points of attachment.
Recall how any ligand bonds to a metal, through donation of a lone pair into an empty metal orbital.
walkthrough:
Picture two teeth biting the metal**
Think of en, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, it has two nitrogen atoms, each with a lone pair. Like a creature with two teeth, it can grip the $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ at two points at once.

Name the bond type**
Each N lone pair is donated into a vacant orbital on the metal, forming a coordinate or dative covalent bond. So a bidentate ligand uses two lone pairs to form two coordinate bonds to the same metal ion.
Final answer: A species that donates two lone pairs to a central metal ion, forming two coordinate (dative covalent) bonds.

hints: Compare $7.94 \times 10^7$ with $3.98 \times 10^{10}$ and remember larger Kstab means the complex is more stable and equilibrium lies further right.
walkthrough:
Let the numbers speak**
$K_{\text{stab}}$ for $[\text{Cu}(en)(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^{2+}$ is about 500 times larger than for $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^{2+}$. A larger K means a higher ratio of products to reactants, so equilibrium 2 is driven more to the right. This is the chelate effect, the bidentate en complex is much more stable.
Final answer: Equilibrium 2 lies further to the right than equilibrium 1 / the en complex is more stable.

hints: Think about $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$ with three identical bidentate rings arranged like a propeller, which type of isomerism gives non-superimposable mirror images.
walkthrough:
Recognise the chiral propeller**
With three symmetrical bidentate en ligands in an octahedral arrangement, the complex can twist like a left handed or right handed propeller. The two forms are mirror images that cannot be superimposed, so this is optical isomerism.

hints: Start by sketching an octahedral Ni centre with solid wedges, hashed wedges and straight lines to show 3D geometry.
Remember each en must span adjacent (cis) positions to form a five membered chelate ring, not opposite positions.
Draw the second structure as the mirror image of the first, reversing the propeller twist to show the pair of enantiomers.
walkthrough:
Set up a clear octahedron**
Draw $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ in the centre with six $\text{N}$ donors octahedrally arranged. Use a solid wedge for a bond coming out, a hashed wedge for a bond going back, and normal lines for in plane bonds. This 3D convention is essential for credit.

Add three en chelates correctly**
Each en is $\text{N-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-N}$, so join two adjacent N positions with a $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-$ bridge to make a five membered ring. Do this three times to surround Ni. Never draw en spanning trans positions, the chain is too short.

Create the mirror image pair**
Now draw the second isomer as the mirror image of the first. If the first has the rings twisting clockwise, the second twists anticlockwise. Label them as the two optical isomers, they are not superimposable, just like left and right hands.
Final answer: Two 3D octahedral structures, each with three en ligands bridging cis positions, drawn as non-superimposable mirror images with wedge / hashed bonds.

hints: Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base in terms of protons, not hydroxide.
Look at the nitrogen atoms in $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and identify what feature allows them to bond to $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Define the base role**
A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. It does not have to contain $\text{OH}^-$, it just needs to take $\text{H}^+$ from an acid.

Find the proton acceptor in en**
Each $-\text{NH}_2$ group has a nitrogen with a lone pair. That lone pair can form a dative bond to $\text{H}^+$, giving $-\text{NH}_3^+$. Since en has two such groups, it can accept two protons overall.
Final answer: Each amino N has a lone pair that can accept / receive a proton ($\text{H}^+$).

hints: Since en has two basic -NH2 groups and HCl is in excess, consider how many moles of HCl react per mole of diamine.
walkthrough:
Protonate both ends**
Excess acid means both $-\text{NH}_2$ groups are protonated. Each takes one $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCl}$: $$\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{ClH}_3\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_3\text{Cl}$$ This can also be written ionically as $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{N}^+\text{H}_3$.

hints: Identify the reacting groups, -COOH from ethanedioic acid and -NH2 from the diamine, and recall what linkage they form with loss of water.
Join them alternately to show two complete amide links on each side, using continuation bonds at the ends to indicate a polymer.
walkthrough:
Make the amide link**
A carboxylic acid plus an amine gives an amide plus water: $-\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{N}- \rightarrow -\text{CONH}- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Here ethanedioic acid is $\text{HO}_2\text{C-CO}_2\text{H}$, so each molecule provides two $\text{C=O}$ groups.

Build two repeat units**
Alternate diamine and diacid residues: $$\text{-NH-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-NH-CO-CO-NH-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-NH-CO-CO-}$$ Draw the $\text{-CO-NH-}$ amide groups displayed fully, with continuation bonds at both ends to show the chain continues. Showing two repeats proves you understand the alternating pattern.
Final answer: Polyamide with repeat: $\text{-[NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCOCO]-}$ shown over two repeat units with $\text{-CONH-}$ amide links and continuation bonds.

hints: Notice that water is eliminated when each amide bond forms, which distinguishes this from addition polymerisation.
walkthrough:
Name by small molecule loss**
Because each new $\text{-CONH-}$ bond releases a small $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecule, monomers join with loss of mass. That is the hallmark of condensation polymerisation, also described mechanistically as addition-elimination.
Final answer: condensation (addition-elimination accepted)

hints: Think of a common addition polymer with a pure carbon chain and no polar hydrolysable links, such as carrier bags or bottles.
walkthrough:
Pick a C-C chain polymer**
Polymer Z is a polyamide with polar $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ links that water and enzymes can hydrolyse, so it biodegrades. A non-biodegradable polymer has a non-polar all carbon backbone with no hydrolysable bond, for example poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC or polystyrene.
Final answer: poly(ethene) / poly(propene) / PVC / polystyrene (any polyalkene)
